title: Why Does Ice Float?
pause_note: 'long' lists beat indices followed by a pause; Short: 0.6 s

beats: Most solids sink in their own liquid. Frozen water does the opposite.
Water molecules are tiny V shapes that cling to each other with hydrogen bonds.
In liquid water, those bonds break and re-form all the time, so the molecules can crowd close.
Freeze it, and each molecule locks onto four neighbours, in an open, six-sided pattern.
That pattern holds more empty space. Ice takes up about nine percent more room than the water, so it floats.
Lucky for fish: lakes freeze from the top, and the ice shields the water below.
Ice floats because freezing locks water's molecules into a roomier pattern.
